meta.title: Who really said "If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. P. Morgan gets the credit, but the wording is posthumous. The earliest known form is a 1926 Wall Street Journal yacht story, 13 years after he died.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Morgan's words. The 1926 Wall Street Journal version reads 'If there is any doubt in your mind, you can't.' Keyes: 'Morgan's sentiments, not his words.'

answer.label: Not Morgan’s words — a posthumous paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is Morgan’s; this sentence is not. The earliest known form of the yacht story appears in The Wall Street Journal on 14 September 1926 — thirteen years after Morgan died — and has him saying only “If there is any doubt in your mind, you can’t,” which is why Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier returns the verdict “Morgan’s sentiments, not his words.”

source.heading: The earliest documented version — and it is not this one

docMeta.dd: The Wall Street Journal, 14 September 1926, p. 2 — thirteen years after Morgan’s death
“If there is any doubt in your mind, you can’t.”
“Morgan’s sentiments, not his words” — Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier (2006), p. 2

source.excerpt: There are two degrees of millionaires: the kind who can afford a yacht, and those who can’t. At least that is what the late J. P. Morgan seemed to think. … A banker … one day decided he needed only a yacht to round out his possessions. … “John,” he said, “do you think I can afford a yacht?” And the answer was: “If there is any doubt in your mind, you can’t.”
source.trailTitle: How the line got its shape
trail: 14 September 1926 — the first known form. The Wall Street Journal runs “Can You Afford a Yacht?”, in which a banker asks “the late J. P. Morgan” whether he can afford one and gets the reply “If there is any doubt in your mind, you can’t.” Popik transcribes the piece in full ↗

1929–1936 — the anecdote hardens while the wording keeps sliding. The Washington Post has “No man who asks himself that question can afford to own a yacht” (1929); Irvin S. Cobb’s Both Sides of the Street has “If you’re not sure you can, you can’t!” (1930); Winthrop P. Moore’s Yachts: Their Care and Handling has “If you have to consider the cost of running the yacht, then you can’t afford to own one” (1936). Each is dated in Popik’s file ↗

26 April 1938 — the modern phrasing surfaces in print, and in this telling it belongs to nobody. The Evening Independent of St. Petersburg, Florida quotes an unnamed observer on horse racing: “It’s like owning a yacht. If you have to ask the price, you can’t afford one.” No Morgan, no attribution at all — it is simply a saying. See the 1938 citation ↗

26 August 1938 — four months later the near-modern wording is back on Morgan, and already being called famous. The Lima (OH) News notes that a yacht’s upkeep “runs into five figures yearly — which forms the basis for the elder J. P. Morgan’s famous comment, when asked by a friend how much it cost to keep up a yacht: ‘If you have to ask such a question, you can’t afford one.’” Morgan’s name is attached in every dated citation from 1926 on except the April 1938 one. Popik dates this citation too ↗

1961 — the exact modern wording is in print under Morgan’s name in a reference-style source. Wikiquote’s only citation for the familiar wording is Business Education World (Gregg Publishing Company, 1961), and the entry sits under “Attributed,” inside the page’s disputed markers. J. P. Morgan on Wikiquote ↗
source.excerptNote: Two things to notice. The paper already calls him the late J. P. Morgan — this is a story told about a dead man, not a line anyone recorded him saying. And the wording is nothing like the proverb: no “price,” no “afford it,” no epigram.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this wording, because no authored source for it has been found. The sentence first appears in the record as an unattributed yachting saying in a 1938 newspaper, and the reference works that have looked for a Morgan original — Keyes, Shapiro, Strouse — did not find one. The 1926 Wall Street Journal item quoted above is a pre-1931 United States periodical and is free of copyright, but that text is not this line.

author.name: J. P. Morgan
author.kicker: The man the line is pinned on
author.heading: Who was J. P. Morgan?
author.metaLine: 1837–1913 · American financier, banker and art collector
author.bio: John Pierpont Morgan was the most powerful private banker of America’s Gilded Age — the man who assembled General Electric and U.S. Steel and twice helped shore up the federal government’s finances. He was also a conspicuous yachtsman, running a succession of steam yachts named Corsair, which is why so many Gilded Age anecdotes about rich men and price tags eventually drifted onto him. His biographer Jean Strouse is blunt about the mismatch between the man and the maxim: Morgan was, she wrote, “a singularly inarticulate, unreflective man, not likely to come up with a maxim worthy of Oscar Wilde.”

The familiar wording is not documented from Morgan: Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier: Who Said What, Where, and When (New York: St. Martin’s Press, 2006), 2 — “Morgan’s sentiments, not his words.”

copyAttribution: "If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it" — popularly credited to J. P. Morgan (1837–1913), but not in his words. The earliest known form of the yacht anecdote is "Can You Afford a Yacht?", The Wall Street Journal, 14 September 1926, p. 2 — thirteen years after Morgan died — where his reply is only "If there is any doubt in your mind, you can't." Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier (2006), p. 2, finds no dependable evidence for the familiar line: "Morgan's sentiments, not his words."

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most quoted things J. P. Morgan never quite said. The situation is real — Morgan owned yachts, and people did ask him what they cost — but the epigram is a retelling artifact that sharpened over about forty years of newspaper columns.

items.why: Ralph Keyes’s The Quote Verifier (2006) states that no dependable evidence exists that Morgan said this, and that biographer Jean Strouse doubts he did, calling the mot “implausible.” Keyes’s verdict: “Morgan’s sentiments, not his words.” The passage is reproduced in Popik’s file ↗

Keyes notes in passing that “Some attribute the thought to Cornelius Vanderbilt” — offering no source for that version either. It is the same pattern: a Gilded Age name large enough to carry the joke. Keyes, quoted by Popik ↗

A separate strand of the story belongs to Morgan’s son: “Legend at the shipyard credits the phrase ‘If you have to ask, you can’t afford it’ to Morgan, when asked what the yacht cost.” That yacht, Corsair IV, was built in 1930 — seventeen years after the elder Morgan’s death — so any telling that puts the Corsair IV exchange in the father’s mouth is impossible on its face. Wikipedia on J. P. Morgan Jr. ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The closest thing to this on the record is a different sentence. The Yale Book of Quotations gives Morgan, on owning a yacht, as “If it makes the slightest difference to you what it costs, don’t try it” — sourced to a 20 May 1927 letter from W. P. Bonbright to Herbert L. Satterlee, which Jean Strouse found among the papers in the Pierpont Morgan Library. That too is a recollection written down after Morgan’s death; Strouse’s closest on-the-record analogue is Morgan’s reply to oil baron Henry Clay Pierce, “You have no right to own a yacht if you ask that question.” Both are documented in Popik’s file ↗

context.heading: Why this one stuck
lead: Morgan is the perfect host for this joke, which is exactly the problem. He ran a fleet of black steam yachts called Corsair, he was the era’s shorthand for unanswerable money, and he died in 1913 — early enough that by the time the anecdote reached print in 1926 there was nobody left to check it against. Every version in the record is a story someone told about Morgan, never a line anyone took down as he spoke.

What the dated citations actually show is a sentence being polished in public. The 1926 reply is flat and conversational. Over the next decade it picks up rhythm, drops the yacht, and by April 1938 it is also running in the papers as a free-floating proverb with no owner at all. Four months after that it is back on Morgan in near-modern wording, the Lima (OH) News already calling it his famous comment — a finished epigram sharper than anything he is documented as saying.
context.detailsSummary: One more thing the record does not contain
detailsBody: It is sometimes suggested the saying is older than Morgan’s yachts. Popik’s file does log an earlier yachting item — Lawrence Perry’s “The Expense of Yachting” in Frank Leslie’s Popular Monthly, August 1901 — but it contains no such maxim. It is an anecdote about a man who said no one could spend more than $100,000 a year and then bought a steam yacht that cost him $70,000 a year to run. The joke is the same; the sentence is not there. Popik’s own conclusion stands: the first known form of the saying dates to only 1926.

sourcesVerified.claim: Popik's file states Morgan's authorship has been questioned and that the first known form of the saying dates to only 1926; it transcribes the 14 September 1926 Wall Street Journal item ("If there is any doubt in your mind, you can't"), the 1929 Washington Post, Cobb's Both Sides of the Street (1930), the 1934 Cleveland Plain Dealer, Moore's Yachts: Their Care and Handling (1936, "If you have to consider the cost of running the yacht, then you can't afford to own one"), the unattributed 26 April 1938 Evening Independent ("If you have to ask the price, you can't afford one"), the 1938 Lima News, the 1941 New York Times and the 1964 Dallas Morning News; it also reproduces the Yale Book of Quotations p. 537 entry (Bonbright letter to Herbert L. Satterlee, 20 May 1927, via Strouse and the Pierpont Morgan Library) and The Quote Verifier p. 2 entry (no dependable evidence; Strouse calls it implausible and Morgan 'a singularly inarticulate, unreflective man'; the Henry Clay Pierce analogue; Vanderbilt mentioned; verdict 'Morgan's sentiments, not his words'), plus the August 1901 Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly yachting item that contains no such maxim.

Wikiquote lists 'If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it.' under the '== Attributed ==' heading, positioned between {{disputed begin}} and {{disputed end}} markers, cited as 'About purchasing a yacht; quoted in "Business Education World" (Gregg Publishing Company, 1961)'.

J. P. Morgan was born 17 April 1837 in Hartford, Connecticut and died 31 March 1913 in Rome; he was a financier, investment banker and art collector, and owned a succession of yachts named Corsair, with Corsair III serving him until his death in 1913.

Corsair IV was built in 1930 by J. P. Morgan Jr. (born 7 September 1867, died 13 March 1943) at Bath Iron Works in Maine, and the article states: 'Legend at the shipyard credits the phrase "If you have to ask, you can't afford it" to Morgan, when asked what the yacht cost. However, this quote is most often attributed to his father...'

This American Dialect Society listserv post is Barry Popik's own earlier posting of the same research (From: Bapopik at AOL.COM, 22 May 2004); it transcribes the 14 September 1926 Wall Street Journal 'Can You Afford a Yacht?' item ('If there is any doubt in your mind, you can't') and the 6 March 1929 Washington Post version ('No man who asks himself that question can afford to own a yacht'), along with later newspaper appearances tying the phrase to Morgan and yachts.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Ralph Keyes, 'The Quote Verifier: Who Said What, Where, and When' (St. Martin's Press, 2006).
The Internet Archive holds a scan of 'The Yale Book of Quotations', edited by Fred R. Shapiro (Yale University Press, 2006, ISBN 0300107986).

A secondary discussion independently reproducing the Quote Verifier / Strouse findings: no dependable evidence Morgan said the line as normally written, and Strouse's closest on-record analogue being Morgan's reply to oil baron Henry Clay Pierce, 'You have no right to own a yacht if you ask that question.'
